q: Which of the following is a fibrous protein?
x: Keratin of hair and nails has long, parallel chains and is insoluble in water, which is typical of fibrous proteins. Insulin, haemoglobin and albumin are compact, soluble globular proteins.

q: A protein that gives only α-amino acids on complete hydrolysis is classified as a:
x: Simple proteins such as albumin are made of amino acids alone. A conjugated protein (for example a nucleoprotein) also gives a non-protein part on hydrolysis.

q: The tertiary structure of a protein, its overall three-dimensional folding, is held mainly by interactions between:
o: The haem groups of the protein
The side chains (R groups) of its amino acids
x: Tertiary folding is held by disulphide bridges, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic forces between R groups. Links between separate chains describe quaternary structure.

q: Disulphide (–S–S–) bridges that help hold the shape of many proteins are formed between units of the amino acid:
x: Cysteine has an –SH group in its side chain, and two –SH groups can join to form an –S–S– bridge. Glycine, alanine and lysine contain no sulphur.

q: Glycine (Gly) and alanine (Ala) can join in either order, and an amino acid can also join to itself. How many different dipeptides can be formed from these two amino acids?
x: Gly–Gly, Ala–Ala, Gly–Ala and Ala–Gly. Gly–Ala and Ala–Gly are different because the free –NH₂ and –COOH ends are on different units.

q: In sickle-cell haemoglobin, one glutamic acid in each β-chain is replaced by valine, and the protein changes shape and works poorly. This shows that:
o: Only the quaternary structure affects function
Peptide bonds are broken in the faulty protein
The haem groups alone decide the shape of the protein
The amino acid sequence determines a protein's shape and function
x: A change of one amino acid in the primary structure alters the folding and so the function. The peptide bonds are intact; only the sequence differs.

q: Which of the following does NOT denature a protein?
o: Dissolving it in water at room temperature
Adding salts of heavy metals such as Hg²⁺
x: Heat, strong acids and heavy-metal ions disrupt the bonds that hold the folded shape. Simply dissolving a soluble protein in water at room temperature leaves its structure intact.

q: In an α-amino acid, the –NH₂ group is attached to:
o: The carbon atom of the –COOH group itself
The carbon farthest from the –COOH group
An oxygen atom of the –COOH group
The carbon atom that is directly bonded to the –COOH group
x: The α-carbon is the carbon next to the carboxyl group, and in α-amino acids it carries both the –NH₂ group and the side chain R.

q: Insulin, a protein hormone made in the pancreas, controls the:
o: Level of glucose in the blood
x: Insulin lowers blood glucose by helping cells take it up. Oxygen transport is the job of haemoglobin, and muscle contraction that of actin and myosin.

q: Which protein is correctly matched with where it is mainly found?
x: Albumin is the main protein of egg white. Casein is in milk, keratin in hair and nails, and haemoglobin in red blood cells.

q: During blood clotting, the soluble plasma protein that is converted into insoluble threads is:
x: Fibrinogen is converted into insoluble fibrin threads, which trap blood cells to form a clot. Albumin stays in solution in the plasma.

q: Proteins that supply all the essential amino acids are called complete (first-class) proteins. Which food is a good source of such protein?
x: Animal proteins such as those in eggs, milk and meat contain all the essential amino acids. Cereal proteins are short of some of them, such as lysine.

q: Among the main classes of food, proteins are the major dietary source of the element:
x: Carbohydrates and fats contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, while every amino acid contains nitrogen in its amino group.

q: Antibodies, which help defend the body against infection, belong chemically to the:
x: Antibodies are soluble, globular proteins (immunoglobulins) in blood plasma. Keratins are structural fibrous proteins.

q: Excess amino acids are not stored in the body. In the liver their amino groups are removed and the nitrogen is excreted mainly as:
x: Deamination in the liver turns the amino nitrogen into urea, which the kidneys excrete. Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate and contains no nitrogen.

q: Which enzyme, substrate and product match is correct?
x: Maltase hydrolyses maltose into two glucose units. Glucose to ethanol is done by zymase, and urease gives ammonia and carbon dioxide from urea.

q: The enzyme diastase (amylase) acts on starch, giving mainly:
x: Diastase hydrolyses starch into maltose, which maltase can then split into glucose. Glucose and fructose come from sucrose by invertase.

q: Pepsin, a protein-digesting enzyme of the stomach, works best at a pH of about:
x: Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works in the strongly acidic stomach, so its optimum is about pH 2; at pH 7 or above its activity is very low.

q: At a fixed enzyme concentration, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is measured at increasing substrate concentrations. The rate rises and then levels off because:
o: All the active sites become occupied, so the enzyme is saturated
The enzyme is denatured at high substrate concentration
The activation energy rises as more substrate is added
The products react back to form the substrate
x: At low substrate concentration more substrate means more enzyme–substrate complexes. Once every active site is busy, adding substrate cannot raise the rate further.

q: A substance that resembles the substrate and occupies an enzyme's active site, slowing the reaction, is called a:
x: A competitive inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site. Coenzymes and activators help an enzyme work rather than slowing it.

q: Some enzymes work only when a metal ion such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺ is present. Such an inorganic ion is called an enzyme:
x: Inorganic ions that an enzyme needs for activity are activators (inorganic cofactors). A coenzyme is an organic molecule, often made from a vitamin.

q: Invertase hydrolyses sucrose: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose). Complete hydrolysis of 342 g of sucrose gives what mass of glucose? (C 12, H 1, O 16)
x: Sucrose = 342 g mol⁻¹, so 342 g is 1 mol, giving 1 mol of glucose = 180 g. 360 g counts glucose and fructose together.
